questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: Notice that since ${A}^{T}\,A$ is diagonal, the singular values of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\sigma }_{1}={\sigma }_{2}=\sqrt{10}.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$): Seeking non-zero solutions of $({A}^{T}\,A-10I)v=0,$ we obtain the unit eigenvectors 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U,$ $Σ,$ and $V:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{10} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt{10}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -9\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -9\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -30 \\ -30 & 90\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: Notice that from the matrix $Σ,$ we can deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=10$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0$ without solving the characteristic equation.

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=100,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-100I & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -30 \\ -30 & 90\end{aligned}]-100[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-90 & -30 \\ -30 & -10\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-100I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -30 \\ -30 & 90\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}10 & -30 \\ -30 & 90\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-0I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A{A}^{T}$): Since the first singular value is not zero, and we know the corresponding singular right vector, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{10}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{30}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that 

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,‖{u}_{2}‖=1.
$$

 

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}{x}_{1}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get a nonzero solution $[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Normalizing this vector, we finally obtain the  second column of $U:$

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]
$$

\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ \sqrt{2} & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: Notice that from the matrix $Σ,$ we can deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=\sqrt{6}$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0$ without solving the characteristic equation.

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-6I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-0I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A{A}^{T}$): Since the first singular value is not zero, and we know the corresponding singular right vector, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2} \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that 

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,‖{u}_{2}‖=1.
$$

 

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{1}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get a nonzero solution $[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Normalizing this vector, we finally obtain the  second column of $U:$ 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}[\begin{aligned}-\sqrt{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: Notice that since ${A}^{T}\,A$ is diagonal, the singular values of $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\sigma }_{1}={\sigma }_{2}=1.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$): Seeking non-zero solutions of $({A}^{T}\,A-1I)v=0,$ we obtain the unit eigenvectors 

$\,$ ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =1[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =1[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U,$ $Σ,$ and $V:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: Notice that from the matrix $Σ,$ we can deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=2$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=0$ without solving the characteristic equation.

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-4I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-0I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A{A}^{T}$): Since the first singular value is not zero, and we know the corresponding singular right vector, we can compute the first column of $U$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since the second singular value is ${\sigma }_{2}=0$, we can't use the same formula to find the second column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector

$$
{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

such that 

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,‖{u}_{2}‖=1.
$$

 

Solving ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0,$ which is equivalent to

$$
-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}=0,
$$

we get a nonzero solution $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Normalizing this vector, we finally obtain the  second column of $U:$

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$
